Abstract.

We construct a smooth rational affine surface SS with finite automorphism group but with the property that the group of automorphisms of the cylinder S×𝔸2S\times\mathbb{A}^{2} acts infinitely transitively on the complement of a closed subset of codimension at least two. Such a surface SS is in particular rigid but not stably rigid with respect to the Makar-Limanov invariant.

Introduction

A complex affine variety XX is called rigid if it does not admit non trivial algebraic actions of the additive group 𝔾a=𝔾a,ℂ\mathbb{G}_{a}=\mathbb{G}_{a,\mathbb{C}}. This is the case for “most” affine varieties, for instance for every affine curve different from the affine line 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} and for every affine variety whose normalization has non negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension. The notion was actually introduced by Crachiola and Makar-Limanov in [4] under the more algebraic equivalent formulation that the Makar-Limanov invariant ML⁡(X)\mathrm{ML}(X) of XX, which is defined as the algebra consisting of regular functions on XX invariant under all algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions, is equal to the coordinate ring Γ⁡(X,𝒪X)\Gamma(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}) of XX.

Among many important questions concerning this invariant, the understanding of its behavior under the operation consisting of taking cylinders X×𝔸nX\times\mathbb{A}^{n}, n≥1n\geq 1, over a given affine variety XX has focused a lot of attention during the last decade, in connexion with the Zariski Cancellation Problem. Of course, rigidity is lost even when passing to the cylinder X×𝔸1X\times\mathbb{A}^{1} since these admit non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions by translations on the second factor. But one could expect that such actions are essentially the unique possible ones in the sense that the projection prX:X×𝔸1→X\mathrm{pr}_{X}:X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow X is invariant for every 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on X×𝔸1X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}, a property which translates algebraically to the fact that ML⁡(X×𝔸1)=ML⁡(X)\mathrm{ML}(X\times\mathbb{A}^{1})=\mathrm{ML}(X). This property was indeed established by Makar-Limanov [14] and this led to wonder more generally whether a rigid variety is stably rigid in the sense that the equality ML⁡(X×𝔸n)=ML⁡(X)\mathrm{ML}(X\times\mathbb{A}^{n})=\mathrm{ML}(X) holds for arbitrary n≥1n\geq 1. Stable rigidity of smooth affine curves is easily confirmed as a consequence of the fact that a smooth rigid curve does not admit any dominant morphism from the affine line, and more generally every rigid affine curve is in fact stably rigid [4]. Stable rigidity is also known to hold for smooth factorial rigid surfaces by virtue of a result of Crachiola [5], and without any indication of a potential counter-example, it seems that the implicit working conjecture so far has been that every rigid affine variety should be stably rigid.

In this article, we construct a smooth rigid surface SS which fails stable rigidity very badly, the cylinder S×𝔸2S\times\mathbb{A}^{2} being essentially as remote as possible from a rigid variety in terms of richness of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on it. Here “richness” has to be interpreted in the sense of a slight weakening of the notion of flexibility introduced recently in [1, 2] that we call flexibility in codimension one: a normal affine variety XX is said to be flexible in codimension one if for every closed point xx outside a possibly empty closed subset of codimension two in XX, the tangent space Tx​XT_{x}X of XX at xx is spanned by tangent vectors to orbits of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on XX. Clearly, the Makar-Limanov invariant of a variety with this property is trivial, consisting of constant functions only. Now our main result can be stated as follows:

Theorem 1.

Let V⊂ℙ3V\subset\mathbb{P}^{3} be smooth cubic surface and let D=V∩HD=V\cap H be a hyperplane section of VV consisting of the union of a smooth conic and its tangent line. Then S=V∖DS=V\setminus D is a smooth rigid affine surface whose cylinder S×𝔸2S\times\mathbb{A}^{2} is flexible in codimension one.

A noteworthy by-product is that while the automorphism group Aut⁡(S)\mathrm{Aut}(S) of SS is finite, actually isomorphic to ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} if the cubic surface VV is chosen general, Theorem 0.1 in [1] implies that Aut⁡(S×𝔸2)\mathrm{Aut}(S\times\mathbb{A}^{2}) acts infinitely transitively on the complement of a closed subset of codimension at least two in S×𝔸2S\times\mathbb{A}^{2}.

Our construction is inspired by earlier work of Bandman and Makar-Limanov [3] which actually already contained the basic ingredients to construct a counter-example to stable rigidity, in the form of a lifting lemma for 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions which asserts that if q:Z→Y\mathrm{q}:Z\rightarrow Y is a line bundle over a normal affine variety YY then ML⁡(Z)⊆ML⁡(Y)\mathrm{ML}(Z)\subseteq\mathrm{ML}(Y), and an example of a non trivial line bundle p:L→S~\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow\tilde{S} over a smooth rational rigid affine surface S~\tilde{S} for which ML⁡(L)⫋ML⁡(S~)\mathrm{ML}(L)\subsetneqq\mathrm{ML}(\tilde{S}). Indeed, with these informations, the property that ML⁡(S~×𝔸2)\mathrm{ML}(\tilde{S}\times\mathbb{A}^{2}) is a proper sub-algebra of ML⁡(S~)\mathrm{ML}(\tilde{S}) could have been already deduced as follows: letting p′:L′→S~\mathrm{p}^{\prime}:L^{\prime}\rightarrow\tilde{S} be a line bundle representing the class of the inverse of LL in the Picard group of S~\tilde{S}, the lifting lemma applied to the rank 22 vector bundle E=L⊕L′=L×S~L′→S~E=L\oplus L^{\prime}=L\times_{\tilde{S}}L^{\prime}\rightarrow\tilde{S} considered as a line bundle over LL via the first projection implies that ML⁡(E)⊆ML⁡(L)⫋ML⁡(S~)\mathrm{ML}(E)\subseteq\mathrm{ML}(L)\subsetneqq\mathrm{ML}(\tilde{S}). But combined with a result of Pavaman Murthy [15] which asserts in particular that every vector bundle on such a surface S~\tilde{S} is isomorphic to the direct sum of its determinant and a trivial bundle, the construction of EE guarantees that it is isomorphic to the trivial bundle S~×𝔸2\tilde{S}\times\mathbb{A}^{2} and hence that ML⁡(S~×𝔸2)⫋ML⁡(S~)\mathrm{ML}(\tilde{S}\times\mathbb{A}^{2})\subsetneqq\mathrm{ML}(\tilde{S}).

Noting that the aforementioned of Pavaman Murthy also applies to surfaces SS as in Theorem 1, the same construction can be used for its proof provided that such an SS admits a line bundle p:L→S\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow S whose total space is flexible in codimension one, and that flexibility in codimension one lifts to total spaces of line bundles. The lifting property follows easily from the fact that every line bundle admits 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-linearizations, but the existence of a line bundle p:L→S\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow S with the desired property is trickier to establish. To construct such a bundle, we exploit the fact that SS admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration π:S→ℙ1\pi:S\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}, i.e. a faithfully flat morphism with generic fiber isomorphic to affine line. The strategy then consists in constructing a suitable 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibered affine surface πF:SF→ℙ1\pi_{F}:S_{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} flexible in codimension one and to which a variant of the famous Danielewski fiber product trick [6] can be applied to derive the existence of an affine threefold flexible in codimension one and carrying simultaneously the structure of a line bundle over SS and SFS_{F}.

The article is organized as follows. In the first section we review basic results about rigid and flexible affine varieties, with a particular focus on the case of affine surfaces, and we establish that flexibility in codimension one does indeed lift to total spaces of line bundles (see Lemma 4). Section two is devoted to the study of the class of affine surfaces SS considered in Theorem 1 and the construction of their aforementioned flexible mates SFS_{F}. The appropriate variant of the Danielewski fiber product trick needed to achieve the proof of Theorem 1 is discussed in the last section.

1. Preliminaries on (stable) rigidity and flexibility

1.1. Rigid and flexible affine varieties


Given a normal complex affine variety X=Spec⁡(A)X=\mathrm{Spec}(A), we denote by 𝒟​e​rℂ​(𝒪X)≃ℋ​o​mX​(ΩX/ℂ1,𝒪X)\mathcal{D}er_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{O}_{X})\simeq\mathcal{H}om_{X}(\Omega_{X/\mathbb{C}}^{1},\mathcal{O}_{X}) the sheaf of germs of ℂ\mathbb{C}-derivations from 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X} to itself. It is a coherent sheaf of 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-modules whose global sections coincide with elements of the AA-module Derℂ​(A)\mathrm{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A) of ℂ\mathbb{C}-derivations of AA. We denote by LNDℂ​(A)\mathrm{LND}_{\mathbb{C}}(A) the sub-AA-module of Derℂ​(A)\mathrm{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A) generated by locally nilpotent ℂ\mathbb{C}-derivations, i.e. ℂ\mathbb{C}-derivations ∂:A→A\partial:A\rightarrow A for which every element of AA is annihilated by a suitable power of ∂\partial. Recall that such derivations coincide precisely with velocity vector fields of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on XX (see e.g. [12]).

Definition 2.

A normal affine variety X=Spec⁡(A)X=\mathrm{Spec}(A) is called:

a) Rigid if LNDℂ​(A)={0}\mathrm{LND}_{\mathbb{C}}(A)=\left\{0\right\}, equivalently XX does not admit non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions,

b) Flexible in codimension 11, or 11-flexible for short, if the support of the co-kernel of the natural homomorphism LNDℂ​(A)⊗A𝒪X→𝒟​e​rX​(𝒪X)\mathrm{LND}_{\mathbb{C}}(A)\otimes_{A}\mathcal{O}_{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}er_{X}(\mathcal{O}_{X}) has codimension at least 22 in XX.

1.1.

The above definition of 11-flexibility says equivalently that there exists a closed subset Z⊂XZ\subset X of codimension at least 22 such that the restriction of 𝒟​e​rℂ​(𝒪X)\mathcal{D}er_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{O}_{X}) over X∖ZX\setminus Z is generated by elements of LNDℂ​(A)\mathrm{LND}_{\mathbb{C}}(A). A closed point x∈Xx\in X at which the natural homomorphism LNDℂ​(A)⊗A𝒪X,x→𝒟​e​rX​(𝒪X)x\mathrm{LND}_{\mathbb{C}}(A)\otimes_{A}\mathcal{O}_{X,x}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}er_{X}(\mathcal{O}_{X})_{x} is surjective is called a flexible point of XX, this property being equivalent by virtue of Nakayama Lemma to the fact that the Zariski tangent space Tx​XT_{x}X of XX at xx is spanned by the tangent vectors to orbits of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on XX. The set XflexX_{\mathrm{flex}} of flexible points is contained in the regular locus XregX_{\mathrm{reg}} of XX and is invariant under the action of the automorphism group Aut⁡(X)\mathrm{Aut}(X) of XX. In particular, if there exists a flexible point x∈Xx\in X such that the complement of the Aut⁡(X)\mathrm{Aut}(X)-orbit of xx is contained in a closed subset of codimension at least two, then XX is flexible in codimension 11.

1.2.

We warn the reader that our definition of flexibility for a normal affine variety XX is weaker than the one introduced earlier in [1, 2] which asks in addition that Xflex=XregX_{\mathrm{flex}}=X_{\mathrm{reg}}. Since for a 11-flexible variety the set X∖XflexX\setminus X_{\mathrm{flex}} has codimension at least two in XX, this makes essentially no difference for global properties of XX depending on regular functions, for instance the Makar-Limanov invariant of a 11-flexible affine variety is trivial. Furthermore, all the properties of the regular locus of a flexible variety in the sense of loc. cit. hold for the open subset XflexX_{\mathrm{flex}} of a 11-flexible variety XX, for instance the sub-group of Aut⁡(X)\mathrm{Aut}(X) generated by its one-parameter unipotent sub-groups acts infinitely transitively on XflexX_{\mathrm{flex}}.

Clearly, the only 11-flexible affine curve is the affine line 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}. While the classification of flexible affine surfaces in the stronger sense of [1, 2] is not known and most probably quite intricate, 11-flexible surfaces coincide with the so-called Gizatullin surfaces [13] with non constant invertible functions. More precisely, we have the following characterization (see also [1, Example 2.3]).

Theorem 3.

For a normal affine surface SS, the following are equivalent:

a) SS is 11-flexible,

b) SS admits two 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations over 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} with distinct general fibers,

c) Γ⁡(S,𝒪S∗)=ℂ∗\Gamma(S,\mathcal{O}_{S}^{*})=\mathbb{C}^{*} and SS admits a normal projective completion S↪VS\hookrightarrow V whose boundary is a chain of proper smooth rational curves supported on the regular locus of VV.

Proof.

It is well known that every 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration q:S→Cq:S\rightarrow C over a smooth affine curve CC arises as the algebraic quotient morphism q:S→S//𝔾a=Spec(Γ(S,𝒪S)𝔾a)q:S\rightarrow S/\negmedspace/\mathbb{G}_{a}=\mathrm{Spec}(\Gamma(S,\mathcal{O}_{S})^{\mathbb{G}_{a}}) of a non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on SS. In particular, the general fibers of such fibrations coincide with the general orbits of a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on SS. Since a flexible surface admits at least two 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions with distinct general orbits, this provides two 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations on SS with distinct general fibers and whose respective base curves are isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} due to the fact that they are dominated by a general fiber of the other fibration. Conversely, let qi:S→𝔸1q_{i}:S\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,2i=1,2, be 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations on SS associated with a pair of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} on SS with distinct general orbits. Since the morphism q1×q2:S→𝔸2q_{1}\times q_{2}:S\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{2} is quasi-finite [8, Lemma 2.21], it follows on the one hand that general orbits of σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} intersect each other transversally and on the other hand that the intersection S0S_{0} of the fixed point loci of σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} is finite. This implies in turn that every point in S∖S0S\setminus S_{0} can be mapped by an element of the sub-group of Aut⁡(S)\mathrm{Aut}(S) generated by σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} to a point p∈Sp\in S at which a general orbit of σ1\sigma_{1} intersects a general orbit of σ2\sigma_{2} transversally. Such a point pp is certainly flexible. Therefore every point outside the finite closed subset S0S_{0} is a flexible point of SS which proves the equivalence between a) and b). For the equivalence b)⇔\Leftrightarrowc) we refer the reader to [8] (in which the statement of Theorem 2.4 should actually be corrected to read: A normal affine surface with no non constant invertible functions is completable by a zigzag if and only if it admits two 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations whose general fibers do not coincide). ∎

1.2. Stable rigidity/stable flexibility.

1.2.1. Rigidity property for line bundles

1.3.

The total space of a line bundle p:L→X\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow X over an affine affine variety X=Spec⁡(A)X=\mathrm{Spec}(A) always admits 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions by generic translations along the fibers of p\mathrm{p}, associated with locally nilpotent AA-derivations of Γ⁡(L,𝒪L)\Gamma(L,\mathcal{O}_{L}). More precisely, these derivations corresponds to 𝔾a,X\mathbb{G}_{a,X}-actions on LL, i.e. 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on LL by XX-automorphisms, and are in one-to-one correspondence with global sections s∈H0​(X,L)s\in H^{0}(X,L) of LL. Indeed, letting p:L=Spec⁡(Sym⁡(M∨))→X\mathrm{p}:L=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathrm{Sym}(M^{\vee}))\rightarrow X, where M≃H0​(X,L)M\simeq H^{0}(X,L) is a locally free AA-module of rank 11, one has ΩSym⁡(M∨)/A1≃Sym⁡(M∨)⊗AM∨\Omega_{\mathrm{Sym}(M^{\vee})/A}^{1}\simeq\mathrm{Sym}(M^{\vee})\otimes_{A}M^{\vee} and the isomorphism

DerA​(Sym⁡(M∨))≃HomSym⁡(M∨)​(ΩSym⁡(M∨)/A1,Sym⁡(M∨))≃Sym⁡(M∨)⊗AM\mathrm{Der}_{A}(\mathrm{Sym}(M^{\vee}))\simeq\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Sym}(M^{\vee})}(\Omega_{\mathrm{Sym}(M^{\vee})/A}^{1},\mathrm{Sym}(M^{\vee}))\simeq\mathrm{Sym}(M^{\vee})\otimes_{A}M

identifies AA-derivations of Γ⁡(L,𝒪L)≃Sym⁡(M∨)\Gamma(L,\mathcal{O}_{L})\simeq\mathrm{Sym}(M^{\vee}) with global sections of the pull-back p∗​L\mathrm{p}^{*}L of LL to its total space. Since a 𝔾a,X\mathbb{G}_{a,X}-action on LL corresponding to a locally nilpotent AA-derivation ∂\partial of Sym⁡(M∨)\mathrm{Sym}(M^{\vee}) restricts on every fiber of p:L→X\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow X to a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action which is either trivial or a translation, it follows that the corresponding section of p∗​L\mathrm{p}^{*}L is constant along the fibers of p:L→X\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow X whence is the pull-back by p\mathrm{p} of a certain section s∂∈H0​(X,L)s_{\partial}\in H^{0}(X,L). Consersely, every global section s∈H0​(X,L)s\in H^{0}(X,L) gives rise to a 𝔾a,X\mathbb{G}_{a,X}-action on LL defined by σs​(t,ℓ)=ℓ+t​s​(p⁡(ℓ))\sigma_{s}(t,\ell)=\ell+ts(\mathrm{p}(\ell)) where the fiberwise addition and multiplication are given by the vector space structure. More formally, viewing p:L→X\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow X as a locally constant group scheme for the law μ:L×XL→L\mu:L\times_{X}L\rightarrow L induced by the addition of germs of sections, global sections s∈H0​(X,L)s\in H^{0}(X,L) give rise to homomorphisms s:𝔾a,X→Ls:\mathbb{G}_{a,X}\rightarrow L of group schemes over XX whence to 𝔾a,X\mathbb{G}_{a,X}-actions σs=μ∘(s×idL):𝔾a,X×XL→L\sigma_{s}=\mu\circ(s\times\mathrm{id}_{L}):\mathbb{G}_{a,X}\times_{X}L\rightarrow L on LL.

1.4.

Even though they are no longer rigid, it is natural to wonder whether total spaces of line bundles p:L→X\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow X over rigid varieties XX stay “as rigid as possible” in the sense that they do not admit any 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions besides the 𝔾a,X\mathbb{G}_{a,X}-actions described above. For the trivial line bundle prX:X×𝔸1→X\mathrm{pr}_{X}:X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow X, the question was settled affirmatively by Makar-Limanov [14] (see also [12, Proposition 9.23]). Let us briefly recall the argument for the convenience of the reader: viewing Γ⁡(X×𝔸1,𝒪X×𝔸1)=A⁡[x]=⨁i≥0A⋅xi\Gamma(X\times\mathbb{A}^{1},\mathcal{O}_{X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}})=A[x]=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}A\cdot x^{i} as a graded AA-algebra, every nonzero locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial of A⁡[x]A[x] associated with a non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on X×𝔸1X\times\mathbb{A}^{1} decomposes into a finite sum ∂=∑i∈ℤ∂i\partial=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}\partial_{i} of nonzero homogeneous derivations ∂i:A⁡[x]→A⁡[x]\partial_{i}:A[x]\rightarrow A[x] of degree i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, the top homogeneous component ∂m\partial_{m} being itself locally nilpotent. Note that m≥−1m\geq-1 for a nonzero derivation and that derivations of the form a∂xa\partial_{x} for a certain a∈A∖{0}a\in A\setminus\{0\} correspond to the case m=−1m=-1. On the other hand, if m≥0m\geq 0 then ∂m=xm∂~0\partial_{m}=x^{m}\tilde{\partial}_{0} for a certain derivation of degree 00 and since ∂m(x)∈xm+1​A⊂x​A\partial_{m}(x)\in x^{m+1}A\subset xA, xx must belong to the kernel of ∂m\partial_{m}. This implies that ∂~0\tilde{\partial}_{0} is a locally nilpotent derivation of degree 00 whose restriction to A=A⋅x0⊂A⁡[x]A=A\cdot x^{0}\subset A[x] is trivial as XX is rigid. But since since x∈Ker(∂~0)=Ker(∂m)x\in\mathrm{Ker}(\tilde{\partial}_{0})=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_{m}), ∂~0\tilde{\partial}_{0} whence ∂\partial would be the zero derivation, a contradiction.

1.5.

In contrast, as mentioned in the introduction, it was discovered by Bandman and Makar-Limanov [3] that the above property can fail for non trivial line bundles. The fact that the rigid surfaces considered in Theorem 1 admit line bundles p:L→S\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow S with 11-flexible total spaces (see §3.3 below) shows that such total spaces can be in general very far from being rigid.

1.2.2. Lifting flexibility in codimension one to split vector bundles

1.6.

The total space of the trivial line bundle prX:X×𝔸1→X\mathrm{pr}_{X}:X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow X over a 11-flexible (resp. flexible in the sense of [2]) affine variety X=Spec⁡(A)X=\mathrm{Spec}(A) is again 11-flexible (resp. flexible). Indeed, every locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial of AA canonically extends to a locally nilpotent derivation ∂~\tilde{\partial} of A⁡[x]A[x] containing xx in its kernel in such way that the projection prX:X×𝔸1→X\mathrm{pr}_{X}:X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow X is equivariant for the corresponding 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on XX and X×𝔸1X\times\mathbb{A}^{1} respectively. It follows that for every point p∈X×𝔸1p\in X\times\mathbb{A}^{1} dominating a flexible point xx of XX, say for which 𝒟​e​rℂ​(𝒪X)x\mathcal{D}er_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{O}_{X})_{x} is generated by the images of locally nilpotent derivations ∂1,…,∂r\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{r} of AA, the 𝒪X×𝔸1,p\mathcal{O}_{X\times\mathbb{A}^{1},p}-module 𝒟​e​rℂ​(𝒪X×𝔸1)p\mathcal{D}er_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{O}_{X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}})_{p} is generated by the images of ∂~1,…,∂~r\tilde{\partial}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\partial}_{r} together with the image of the locally nilpotent AA-derivation ∂x\partial_{x} of A⁡[x]A[x]. This implies that prX−1​(Xflex)⊂(X×𝔸1)flex\mathrm{pr}_{X}^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{flex}})\subset(X\times\mathbb{A}^{1})_{\mathrm{flex}} and hence that the set of non flexible points in X×𝔸1X\times\mathbb{A}^{1} has codimension at least two. Furthermore, (X×𝔸1)flex(X\times\mathbb{A}^{1})_{\mathrm{flex}} coincides with (X×𝔸1)reg(X\times\mathbb{A}^{1})_{\mathrm{reg}} in the case where Xflex=XregX_{\mathrm{flex}}=X_{\mathrm{reg}}.

1.7.

Even though different results related with lifts of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on an affine variety XX to 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on total spaces of line bundles p:L→X\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow X over it exist in the literature (in particular, [3, Lemma 9] and [1, Corollary 4.5]), it seems that the question whether 11-flexibility or flexibility of XX lifts to total spaces of arbitrary line bundles over it has not been clearly settled yet. This is fixed by the following cost free generalization:

Lemma 4.

Let XX be a normal affine variety and let p:E→X\mathrm{p}:E\rightarrow X be a vector bundle which splits as a direct sum of line bundles. If XX is 11-flexible (resp. flexible) then so is the total space of EE.

Proof.

Since EE is isomorphic to the fiber product L1×XL2⋯×XLrL_{1}\times_{X}L_{2}\cdots\times_{X}L_{r} of line bundles pi:Li→X\mathrm{p}_{i}:L_{i}\rightarrow X, we are reduced by induction to the case of a line bundle p:L→Y\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow Y over a 11-flexible (resp. flexible) affine variety. Recall that for a connected algebraic group GG acting on a normal variety YY, there exists an exact sequence of groups

0→Halg1​(G,Γ⁡(Y,𝒪Y∗))→PicG​(Y)→αPic⁡(Y)→Pic⁡(G)0\rightarrow H_{\mathrm{alg}}^{1}(G,\Gamma(Y,\mathcal{O}_{Y}^{*}))\rightarrow\mathrm{Pic}^{G}(Y)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\alpha}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathrm{Pic}(Y)\rightarrow\mathrm{Pic}(G)

where PicG​(Y)\mathrm{Pic}^{G}(Y) denotes the group of GG-linearized line bundles on YY and where Halg1​(G,Γ⁡(Y,𝒪Y∗))H_{\mathrm{alg}}^{1}(G,\Gamma(Y,\mathcal{O}_{Y}^{*})) parametrizes isomorphy classes of GG-linearizations of the trivial line bundle over YY (see e.g. [7, Chap. 7]). In the case where G=𝔾aG=\mathbb{G}_{a}, this immediately implies that every line bundle p:L→Y\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow Y admits a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-linearization (note furthermore that such a linearization is unique up to isomorphism provided that Γ⁡(Y,𝒪Y∗)=ℂ∗\Gamma(Y,\mathcal{O}_{Y}^{*})=\mathbb{C}^{*}).

It follows in particular that every 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on YY can be lifted to a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on LL preserving the zero section Y0⊂LY_{0}\subset L and for which the structure morphism p:L→Y\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow Y is 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-invariant. So the 11-flexibility (resp. the flexibility) of LL follows from that of YY thanks to [1, Corollary 4.5]. But let us provide a self-contained argument: the above property translates algebraically to the fact that every locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial of Γ⁡(Y,𝒪Y)\Gamma(Y,\mathcal{O}_{Y}) extends to a locally nilpotent derivation ∂~\tilde{\partial} of Γ⁡(L,𝒪L)\Gamma(L,\mathcal{O}_{L}) mapping the ideal IY0I_{Y_{0}} of Y0Y_{0} into itself and such that the induced derivation on Γ⁡(Y0,𝒪Y0)=Γ⁡(L,𝒪L)/IY0\Gamma(Y_{0},\mathcal{O}_{Y_{0}})=\Gamma(L,\mathcal{O}_{L})/I_{Y_{0}} coincides with ∂\partial via the isomorphism Γ⁡(Y,𝒪Y)→∼Γ⁡(Y0,𝒪Y0)\Gamma(Y,\mathcal{O}_{Y})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}\Gamma(Y_{0},\mathcal{O}_{Y_{0}}) induced by the restriction of p\mathrm{p}. Since YY is affine, given any point ℓ∈L\ell\in L, we can find a global section s∈H0​(Y,L)s\in H^{0}(Y,L) which does not vanish at y=p⁡(ℓ)y=\mathrm{p}(\ell). Now if yy is a flexible point of YY, say for which 𝒟​e​rℂ​(𝒪Y)y\mathcal{D}er_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{O}_{Y})_{y} is generated by the images of locally nilpotent derivations ∂1,…,∂r\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{r} of Γ⁡(Y,𝒪Y)\Gamma(Y,\mathcal{O}_{Y}) then ℓ0=p−1​(y)∩Y0\ell_{0}=\mathrm{p}^{-1}(y)\cap Y_{0} is a flexible point of LL at which 𝒟​e​rℂ​(𝒪L)ℓ0\mathcal{D}er_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{O}_{L})_{\ell_{0}} is generated by the lifts ∂~1,…,∂~r\tilde{\partial}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\partial}_{r} of ∂1,…,∂r\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{r} together with the locally nilpotent derivation ∂s\partial_{s} of Γ⁡(L,𝒪L)\Gamma(L,\mathcal{O}_{L}) corresponding to the 𝔾a,Y\mathbb{G}_{a,Y}-action σs:𝔾a,Y×YL→L\sigma_{s}:\mathbb{G}_{a,Y}\times_{Y}L\rightarrow L associated with ss (see §1.3 above). Furthermore, since ss does vanish at yy, the 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action induced by σs\sigma_{s} on p−1​(y)\mathrm{p}^{-1}(y) is transitive, and so p−1​(y)\mathrm{p}^{-1}(y) consists of flexible points of LL. This shows that p−1​(Yflex)⊂Lflex\mathrm{p}^{-1}(Y_{\mathrm{flex}})\subset L_{\mathrm{flex}} and completes the proof. ∎

2. Construction of rigid and 11-flexible 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibered surfaces over over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}

In this section, we first consider affine surfaces SRS_{R} which arise as complements of well-chosen hyperplane sections of a smooth cubic surface in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}. We check that they are rigid by computing their automorphism groups and we exhibit certain 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations πR:SR→ℙ1\pi_{R}:S_{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} on them. We then construct auxiliary 11-flexible 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibered surfaces πF:SF→ℙ1\pi_{F}:S_{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} which will be used later on in section three for the proof of Theorem 1.

2.1. A family of rigid affine cubic surfaces

Most of the material of this sub-section is borrowed from [10] to which we refer the reader for the details.

2.1.

Given a smooth cubic surface V⊂ℙ3V\subset\mathbb{P}^{3} and a line LL on it, the restriction to VV of the linear pencil ℋL=|𝒪ℙ3​(1)⊗ℐL|\mathcal{H}_{L}=\left|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{3}}(1)\otimes\mathcal{I}_{L}\right| on ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} generated by planes containing LL can be decomposed as ℋL∣V=ℒ+L\mathcal{H}_{L}\mid_{V}=\mathcal{L}+L where ℒ\mathcal{L} is a base point free pencil defining a conic bundle Φℒ:V→ℙ1\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with five degenerate fibers each consisting of the union of two lines. The restriction Φℒ∣L:L→ℙ1\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}\mid_{L}:L\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} is a double cover and for every branch point x∈ℙ1x\in\mathbb{P}^{1} of Φℒ∣L\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}\mid_{L}, the intersection of VV with the corresponding hyperplane Hx∈ℋH_{x}\in\mathcal{H} consists either of a smooth conic tangent to LL or two distinct lines intersecting LL in a same point, which is then an Eckardt point of VV. The second case does not occur if VV is chosen general. We fix from now on a cubic surface VV, a line LL on it and a hyperplane section D=H∩VD=H\cap V for which D=L+CD=L+C where CC is a smooth conic tangent to LL at a point p∈Lp\in L.

2.2.

Given a pair (V,D)\left(V,D\right) where D=L+CD=L+C as above, the surface SR=V∖DS_{R}=V\setminus D is affine as DD is a hyperplane section of VV. It comes equipped with an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πR:SR→ℙ1\pi_{R}:S_{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} which is obtained as follows: we let μ:V→ℙ2\mu:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} be the birational morphism obtained by contracting a 66-tuple of disjoint lines L,F1,…,F5⊂VL,F_{1},\ldots,F_{5}\subset V with the property that each FiF_{i}, i=1,…,5i=1,\ldots,5, intersects CC transversally. Since LL is tangent to CC, the image μ∗​(C)\mu_{*}(C) of CC in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} is a cuspidal cubic. The rational pencil on ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} generated by μ∗​(C)\mu_{*}(C) and three times its tangent TT at its unique singular point μ⁡(p)\mu(p) lifts to a rational pencil q¯:V⇢ℙ1\overline{q}:V\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} having the divisors C+∑i=15FiC+\sum_{i=1}^{5}F_{i} and 3​T+L3T+L as singular members. Letting τ:V^→V\tau:\hat{V}\rightarrow V be a minimal resolution of q¯\overline{q}, the induced morphism q¯∘τ:V^→ℙ1\overline{q}\circ\tau:\hat{V}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} is a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration whose restriction to SR=V∖D≃V^∖τ−1​DS_{R}=V\setminus D\simeq\hat{V}\setminus\tau^{-1}D is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πR:SR→ℙ1\pi_{R}:S_{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with two degenerate fibers: one is irreducible of multiplicity three consisting of the intersection of the proper transform of TT with SRS_{R} and the other is reduced, consisting of the disjoint union of the curves Fi∩SR≃𝔸1F_{i}\cap S_{R}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,…,5i=1,\ldots,5 (see Figure 2.1).

Remark 5.

Choosing an alternative 66-tuple of disjoint lines F0,1​F0,2,F∞,1,…,F∞,4F_{0,1}F_{0,2},F_{\infty,1},\ldots,F_{\infty,4} such that F∞,1,…,F∞,4F_{\infty,1},\ldots,F_{\infty,4} intersect CC transversally while F0,1F_{0,1} and F0,2F_{0,2} intersects LL but not CC, we obtain another contraction morphism μ~:V→ℙ2\tilde{\mu}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} for which the proper transforms of CC and LL are respectively a conic and its tangent line at the point μ~​(p)\tilde{\mu}(p). One checks that the lift to VV of the rational pencil on ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} generated by μ~∗​(C)\tilde{\mu}_{*}(C) and 2​μ∗​(L)2\mu_{*}(L) restricts on SRS_{R} to an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πR′:SR→ℙ1\pi^{\prime}_{R}:S_{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with two reducible degenerate fibers: one consisting of the disjoint union of the curves F0,i∩S≃𝔸1F_{0,i}\cap S\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,2i=1,2, both occuring with multiplicity two and the other one consisting of the disjoint union of the reduced curves F∞,i∩SR≃𝔸1F_{\infty,i}\cap S_{R}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,…,4i=1,\ldots,4. The description of the degenerate fibers shows that this second 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration is not isomorphic to the one πR:SR→ℙ1\pi_{R}:S_{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}, so that SRS_{R} carries at least two distinct types of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}.

2.3.

To determine the automorphism group of SR=V∖DS_{R}=V\setminus D we first notice that the subgroup Aut⁡(V,D)\mathrm{Aut}(V,D) of Aut⁡(V)\mathrm{Aut}(V) consisting of automorphisms of VV which leave DD globally invariant can be identified in a natural way with a subgroup of Aut⁡(SR)\mathrm{Aut}(S_{R}). The latter is always finite, and even trivial if the cubic surface VV is chosen general. On the other hand, SRS_{R} admits at least another natural automorphism which is obtained as follows: the projection ℙ3⇢ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{3}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} from the point p=L∩Cp=L\cap C induces a rational map Q⇢ℙ2Q\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} with pp as a unique proper base point and whose lift to the blow-up α:W→V\alpha:W\rightarrow V of VV at pp coincides with the morphism θ:W→ℙ2\theta:W\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} defined by the anticanonical linear system |−KW||-K_{W}|. The latter factors into a birational morphism W→YW\rightarrow Y contracting the proper transform of LL followed by a Galois double cover Y→ℙ2Y\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} ramified over an irreducible quartic curve Δ\Delta with a unique double point located at the image of LL. The non trivial involution of the double cover Y→ℙ2Y\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} induces an involution GW:W→WG_{W}:W\rightarrow W fixing LL and exchanging the proper transform of CC with the exceptional divisor EE of α\alpha. The former descends to a birational involution GV,p:V⇢VG_{V,p}:V\dashrightarrow V which restricts further to a biregular involution jGV,pj_{G_{V,p}} of SR=V∖DS_{R}=V\setminus D.

The following description of the automorphism group of SRS_{R} shows in particular that these surfaces are rigid:

Lemma 6.

For a surface SR=V∖DS_{R}=V\setminus D as above, there exists a split exact sequence

0→Aut⁡(V,D)→Aut⁡(SR)→ℤ2⋅jGV,p→0.0\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(V,D)\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(S_{R})\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{2}\cdot j_{G_{V,p}}\rightarrow 0.
Proof.

We interpret every automorphism of SRS_{R} as a birational self-map f:V⇢Vf:V\dashrightarrow V of VV restricting to an isomorphism from SR=V∖DS_{R}=V\setminus D to itself. Since f∈Aut⁡(V,D)f\in\mathrm{Aut}(V,D) in case it is biregular, it is enough to show that either ff or GV,p∘fG_{V,p}\circ f is biregular. To establish this alternative, it suffices to check that the lift fW=α−1​f​α:W⇢Wf_{W}=\alpha^{-1}f\alpha:W\dashrightarrow W of ff to WW is a biregular morphism, hence an automorphism of the pair (W,α−1​(D)red)(W,\alpha^{-1}(D)_{\mathrm{red}}). Indeed if so, then fWf_{W} preserves the union of EE and the proper transform of DD as these are the only (−1)\left(-1\right)-curves contained in the support of α−1​(D)red\alpha^{-1}(D)_{\mathrm{red}}. Since by construction GWG_{W} exchanges EE and the proper transform of DD, it follows that either fWf_{W} or GW∘fWG_{W}\circ f_{W} leaves EE, the proper transform of DD and the proper transform of LL invariant. This implies in turn that either f=α​fW​α−1f=\alpha f_{W}\alpha^{-1} or α​GW∘fW​α−1=(α​GW​α−1)∘(α​fW​α−1)=GV,p∘f\alpha G_{W}\circ f_{W}\alpha^{-1}=(\alpha G_{W}\alpha^{-1})\circ(\alpha f_{W}\alpha^{-1})=G_{V,p}\circ f is a biregular automorphism of VV.

To show that fWf_{W} is a biregular automorphism of WW, we consider the lift f~=σ−1∘f∘σ:V~⇢V~\tilde{f}=\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma:\tilde{V}\dashrightarrow\tilde{V} of ff to the variety α~:V~→W\tilde{\alpha}:\tilde{V}\rightarrow W obtained from WW by blowing-up further the intersection point of EE and of the proper transform of CC, say with exceptional divisor E~\tilde{E}. We identify SRS_{R} with the complement in V~\tilde{V} of the SNC divisor D~=L∪C∪E∪E~\tilde{D}=L\cup C\cup E\cup\tilde{E}. Now suppose by contradiction that f~\tilde{f} is strictly birational and consider its minimal resolution V~←βX→β′V~′\tilde{V}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\beta}}{{\leftarrow}}X\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\beta^{\prime}}}{{\rightarrow}}\tilde{V}^{\prime}. Recall that the minimality of the resolution implies in particular that there is no (−1)\left(-1\right)-curve in XX which is exceptional for β\beta and β′\beta^{\prime} simultaneously. Furthermore, since V~\tilde{V} is smooth and D~\tilde{D} is an SNC divisor, β′\beta^{\prime} decomposes into a finite sequence of blow-downs of successive (−1)\left(-1\right)-curves supported on the boundary B=β−1​(D~)red=(β′)−1​(D~)redB=\beta^{-1}(\tilde{D})_{\mathrm{red}}=(\beta^{\prime})^{-1}(\tilde{D})_{\mathrm{red}} with the property that at each step, the proper transform of BB is again an SNC divisor. The structure of D~\tilde{D} implies that the only possible (−1)\left(-1\right)-curve in BB which is not exceptional for β\beta is the proper transform of E~\tilde{E}, but after its contraction, the proper transform of BB would no longer be an SNC divisor, a contradiction. So f~:V~→V~\tilde{f}:\tilde{V}\rightarrow\tilde{V} is a morphism and the same argument shows that it does not contract any curve in the boundary D~\tilde{D}. Thus f~\tilde{f} is a biregular automorphism of V~\tilde{V}, in fact, an element of Aut⁡(V~,D~)\mathrm{Aut}(\tilde{V},\tilde{D}). Since E~\tilde{E} is the unique (−1)\left(-1\right)-curve contained in the support of D~\tilde{D} it must be invariant by f~\tilde{f} which implies in turn that fW=α~​f~​α~−1f_{W}=\tilde{\alpha}\tilde{f}\tilde{\alpha}^{-1} is a biregular automorphism of the pair (W,α−1​(D)red)(W,\alpha^{-1}(D)_{\mathrm{red}}), as desired. ∎

2.2. Flexible mates

In this subsection, we construct 11-flexible affine surfaces SFS_{F} admitting 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations πF:SF→ℙ1\pi_{F}:S_{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} whose degenerate fibers resemble the ones of the fibrations πR:SR→ℙ1\pi_{R}:S_{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} described in §2.2 above. A more precise interpretation of this resemblance, going beyond the bare fact that the number of their irreducible components and their respective multiplicities are the same, will be given in the next section.

2.4.

For the construction, we start with a Hirzebruch surface πn:𝔽n=ℙ⁡(𝒪ℙ1⊕𝒪ℙ1​(−n))→ℙ1\pi_{n}:\mathbb{F}_{n}=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-n))\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}, n≥0n\geq 0, in which we fix an ample section C≃ℙ1C\simeq\mathbb{P}^{1} of πn\pi_{n} and two distinct fibers, say F0=πn−1​(p0)F_{0}=\pi_{n}^{-1}(p_{0}) and F∞=πn−1​(p∞)F_{\infty}=\pi_{n}^{-1}(p_{\infty}), where p0,p∞∈ℙ1p_{0},p_{\infty}\in\mathbb{P}^{1} . We let σ:X→𝔽n\sigma:X\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{n} be the birational map obtained by the following sequence of blow-ups:

- Step 1 consists of the blow-up of five distinct points p∞,1,…,p∞,5p_{\infty,1},\ldots,p_{\infty,5} on F∞∖CF_{\infty}\setminus C with respective exceptional divisors G∞,1,…,G∞,5G_{\infty,1},\ldots,G_{\infty,5}.

- Step 2 consists of the blow-up of a point p0,1∈F0∖Cp_{0,1}\in F_{0}\setminus C with exceptional divisor E1E_{1}, followed by the blow-up of the intersection point p0,2p_{0,2} of the proper transform of F0F_{0} with E1E_{1}, with exceptional divisor E2E_{2}, then followed by the blow-up of the intersection point p0,3p_{0,3} of the proper transform of F0F_{0} with E2E_{2}, with exceptional divisor E3E_{3}. Finally, we blow-up a point p0,4∈E3p_{0,4}\in E_{3} distinct from the intersection points of E3E_{3} with the proper transforms of F0F_{0} and E2E_{2} respectively. We denote the last exceptional divisor produced by G0,1G_{0,1}.

The structure morphism πn:𝔽n→ℙ1\pi_{n}:\mathbb{F}_{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} lifts to a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration p¯=πn∘σ:X→ℙ1\overline{p}=\pi_{n}\circ\sigma:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with two degenerate fibers p¯−1​(p0)=F0+E1+2​E2+3​E3+3​G0,1\overline{p}^{-1}(p_{0})=F_{0}+E_{1}+2E_{2}+3E_{3}+3G_{0,1} and p¯−1​(p∞)=F∞+∑i=15G∞,i\overline{p}^{-1}(p_{\infty})=F_{\infty}+\sum_{i=1}^{5}G_{\infty,i}. The inverse image by σ\sigma of the divisor F0∪C∪F∞F_{0}\cup C\cup F_{\infty} is pictured in Figure 2.2. Letting SFS_{F} be the open complement in XX of the divisor B=F∞∪C∪F0∪E3∪E2∪E1B=F_{\infty}\cup C\cup F_{0}\cup E_{3}\cup E_{2}\cup E_{1}, the restriction of p¯\overline{p} to SFS_{F} is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πF:SF→ℙ1\pi_{F}:S_{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with two degenerate fibers: the one πF−1​(p0)\pi_{F}^{-1}(p_{0}) is irreducible of multiplicity three consisting of the intersection of G0,1G_{0,1} with SFS_{F} and the other one πF−1​(p∞)\pi_{F}^{-1}(p_{\infty}) is reduced, consisting of the disjoint union of the curves G∞,i∩SF≃𝔸1G_{\infty,i}\cap S_{F}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,…,5i=1,\ldots,5.

Lemma 7.

A surface SF=X∖BS_{F}=X\setminus B as above is affine and 11-flexible.

Proof.

By construction, BB is chain of smooth complete rational curves. So the 11-flexibility of SFS_{F} will follows from Theorem 3 provided that SFS_{F} is indeed affine and has no non constant invertible functions. Since πF:SF→ℙ1\pi_{F}:S_{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration, an invertible function on SFS_{F} is constant in restriction to every non degenerate fiber of πF\pi_{F} and hence has the form f∘πFf\circ\pi_{F} for a certain global invertible function ff on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. So such a function is certainly constant. To establish the affineness of SFS_{F}, we first observe that SFS_{F} does not contain a complete curve. Indeed, otherwise since the points blown-up by σ:X→𝔽n\sigma:X\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{n} are contained in 𝔽n∖C\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus C, the image by σ\sigma of such curve would be a complete curve in 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n} which does not intersect CC, in contradiction with the ampleness of CC in 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n}. On the other hand, since CC has positive self-intersection in 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n}, whence in XX, one checks by direct computation that for a∞,a,a0,a1,a2,a3∈ℤ>0a_{\infty},a,a_{0},a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} such that a0≫a3≫a2≫a1a_{0}\gg a_{3}\gg a_{2}\gg a_{1} and a≫max⁡(a0,a∞)a\gg\max(a_{0},a_{\infty}), the effective divisor B~=a∞​F∞+a​C+a0​F0+a1​E1+a2​E2+a3​E3\tilde{B}=a_{\infty}F_{\infty}+aC+a_{0}F_{0}+a_{1}E_{1}+a_{2}E_{2}+a_{3}E_{3} has positive self-intersection and positive intersection which each of its irreducible components. It then follows from the Nakai-Moishezon criterion that B~\tilde{B} is an ample effective divisor supported on BB, and hence that SF=X∖BS_{F}=X\setminus B is affine. ∎

Remark 8.

In the construction of §2.4, one can replace Step 1 and 2 by the following alternative sequence of blow-ups σ′:X′→𝔽n\sigma^{\prime}:X^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{n}:

- Step 1’ consists of the blow-up of four distinct points p∞,1′,…,p∞,4′p^{\prime}_{\infty,1},\ldots,p^{\prime}_{\infty,4} on F∞∖CF_{\infty}\setminus C with respective exceptional divisors G∞,1′,…,G∞,4′G^{\prime}_{\infty,1},\ldots,G^{\prime}_{\infty,4}.

- Step 2’ consists of the blow-up of a point p0,1′∈F0∖Cp^{\prime}_{0,1}\in F_{0}\setminus C with exceptional divisor E1′E_{1}^{\prime}, followed by the blow-up of the intersection point p0,2′p^{\prime}_{0,2} of the proper transform of F0F_{0} with E1′E^{\prime}_{1}, with exceptional divisor E2′E^{\prime}_{2}, then followed by the blow-up of a pair of distinct points p0,3′p^{\prime}_{0,3} and p0,3′′p^{\prime\prime}_{0,3} on E2′E_{2}^{\prime} distinct from the intersection points of E2′E_{2}^{\prime} with the proper transforms of F0F_{0} and E1′E_{1}^{\prime}, with respective exceptional divisors G0,1′G^{\prime}_{0,1} and G0,2′G^{\prime}_{0,2}.

The morphism p¯′=πn∘σ′:X′→ℙ1\overline{p}^{\prime}=\pi_{n}\circ\sigma^{\prime}:X^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} is then a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration with two degenerate fibers p¯′−1​(p0)=F0+E1′+2​E2′+2​G0,1′+2​G0,2′{\overline{p}^{\prime}}^{-1}(p_{0})=F_{0}+E^{\prime}_{1}+2E^{\prime}_{2}+2G^{\prime}_{0,1}+2G^{\prime}_{0,2} and p¯′−1​(p∞)=F∞+∑i=14G∞,i′{\overline{p}^{\prime}}^{-1}(p_{\infty})=F_{\infty}+\sum_{i=1}^{4}G^{\prime}_{\infty,i}. The same argument as in the proof of Lemma 7 above shows that the complement in X′X^{\prime} of the chain of smooth complete rational curves B′=F∞∪C∪F0∪E1′∪E2′B^{\prime}=F_{\infty}\cup C\cup F_{0}\cup E_{1}^{\prime}\cup E_{2}^{\prime} is a 11-flexible affine surface, on which p¯′\overline{p}^{\prime} restricts to an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πF′:SF′→ℙ1\pi^{\prime}_{F}:S^{\prime}_{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with two degenerate fibers consisting respectively of the disjoint union of G0,i′∩SF′≃𝔸1G^{\prime}_{0,i}\cap S^{\prime}_{F}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,2i=1,2 both occurring with multiplicity 22 and of the disjoint union of the reduced curves G∞,i′∩SF′≃𝔸1G^{\prime}_{\infty,i}\cap S^{\prime}_{F}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,…,4i=1,\ldots,4. So πF′:SF′→ℙ1\pi^{\prime}_{F}:S^{\prime}_{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} resembles the alternative 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πR′:SR→ℙ1\pi^{\prime}_{R}:S_{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} described in Remark 5 above.

3. rigidity lost

The last ingredient needed to derive Theorem 1 is the following result:

Proposition 9.

Let πR:SR→ℙ1\pi_{R}:S_{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} and πF:SF→ℙ1\pi_{F}:S_{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} be a pair of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibered surfaces as constructed in §2.2 and 2.4 above. Then there exists an algebraic space δ:ℭ→ℙ1\delta:\mathfrak{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} such that πR\pi_{R} and πF\pi_{F} factor respectively through étale locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundles ρR:SR→ℭ\rho_{R}:S_{R}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} and ρF:SF→ℭ\rho_{F}:S_{F}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C}.

Let us first explain how derive the 11-flexibility of the cylinder SF×𝔸2S_{F}\times\mathbb{A}^{2} from this Proposition.

3.1.

Recall that since the automorphism group of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} is the affine group Aff1=𝔾m⋉𝔾a\mathrm{Aff}_{1}=\mathbb{G}_{m}\ltimes\mathbb{G}_{a}, every étale locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle ρ:S→ℭ\rho:S\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} is in fact an affine-linear bundle. This means that there exists a line bundle p:L→ℭ\mathrm{p}:L\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} such that ρ:S→ℭ\rho:S\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} has the structure of an étale LL-torsor, that is, an étale locally trivial principal homogeneous bundle under LL, considered as a group space over ℭ\mathfrak{C} for the group law induced by the addition of germs of sections. Isomorphy classes of such principal homogeneous LL-bundles are then classified by the cohomology group He´​t1​(ℭ,L)H_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}^{1}(\mathfrak{C},L) (see e.g. [9, §1.2]).

3.2.

So Proposition 9 implies in particular that ρR:SR→ℭ\rho_{R}:S_{R}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} and ρF:SF→ℭ\rho_{F}:S_{F}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} can be equipped with the structure of principal homogeneous bundles under suitable line bundles pR:LR→ℭ\mathrm{p}_{R}:L_{R}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} and pF:LF→ℭ\mathrm{p}_{F}:L_{F}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} respectively. As a consequence, the fiber product Z=SR×ℭSFZ=S_{R}\times_{\mathfrak{C}}S_{F} is simultaneously equipped via the first and second projection with the structure of a principal homogeneous bundle under the line bundles ρR∗​LF\rho_{R}^{*}L_{F} and ρF∗​LR\rho_{F}^{*}L_{R} respectively. But since SRS_{R} and SFS_{F} are both affine, the vanishing of He´​t1​(SR,ρR∗​LF)H_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}^{1}(S_{R},\rho_{R}^{*}L_{F}) and He´​t1​(SF,ρF∗​LR)H_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}^{1}(S_{F},\rho_{F}^{*}L_{R}) implies that pr1:Z→SR\mathrm{pr}_{1}:Z\rightarrow S_{R} and pr2:Z→SF\mathrm{pr}_{2}:Z\rightarrow S_{F} are the trivial ρR∗​LF\rho_{R}^{*}L_{F}-torsor and ρF∗​LR\rho_{F}^{*}L_{R}-torsor respectively. In other word, ZZ carries simultaneously the structure of a line bundle over SRS_{R} and SFS_{F}.

3.3.

Now since SFS_{F} is 11-flexible by virtue of Theorem 3, we deduce from Lemma 4 that ZZ is 11-flexible. Furthermore, the same Lemma implies that given any line bundle p:Z′→SR\mathrm{p}:Z^{\prime}\rightarrow S_{R}, the total space of the rank 22 vector bundle pr1×p:E=Z′×XZ→SR\mathrm{pr}_{1}\times\mathrm{p}:E=Z^{\prime}\times_{X}Z\rightarrow S_{R} over SRS_{R} is 11-flexible. On the other hand, it follows from [15, Theorem 3.2] that every rank 22 vector bundle E→SRE\rightarrow S_{R} splits a trivial factor, whence is isomorphic to the direct sum of its determinant detE\det E and of the trivial line bundle. Choosing for Z′Z^{\prime} a line bundle representing the inverse of the class of pr1:Z→SR\mathrm{pr}_{1}:Z\rightarrow S_{R} in the Picard group Pic⁡(SR)\mathrm{Pic}(S_{R}) of SRS_{R} yields a vector bundle E=Z′×XZ→SRE=Z^{\prime}\times_{X}Z\rightarrow S_{R} with trivial determinant, whence isomorphic to the trivial one SR×𝔸2S_{R}\times\mathbb{A}^{2}, and with 11-flexible total space.

3.1. Proof of Proposition 9

3.4.

To prove Proposition 9, we first observe that if it exists, an algebraic space δ:ℭ→ℙ1\delta:\mathfrak{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with the property that a given 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration π:S→ℙ1\pi:S\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} on a smooth surface SS factors as δ∘ρ\delta\circ\rho, where ρ:S→ℭ\rho:S\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} is an étale locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle, is unique up to isomorphism of spaces over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. Indeed, suppose that δ′:ℭ→ℙ1\delta^{\prime}:\mathfrak{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} is another such space for which we have π=δ′∘ρ′\pi=\delta^{\prime}\circ\rho^{\prime} where ρ′:S′→ℭ′\rho^{\prime}:S^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} is an étale locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle. The closed fibers of ρ\rho and ρ′\rho^{\prime} being both in one-to-one correspondence with irreducible components of closed fibers of π\pi, it follows that for every closed point c∈ℭc\in\mathfrak{C} there exists a unique closed point c′∈ℭ′c^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} such that δ⁡(c)=δ′​(c′)\delta(c)=\delta^{\prime}(c^{\prime}) and ρ−1​(c)=(ρ′)−1​(c′)⊂π−1​(δ⁡(c))\rho^{-1}(c)=(\rho^{\prime})^{-1}(c^{\prime})\subset\pi^{-1}(\delta(c)). So the correspondence c↦c′c\mapsto c^{\prime} defines a bijection ψ:ℭ→ℭ′\psi:\mathfrak{C}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} such that ρ′=ψ∘ρ\rho^{\prime}=\psi\circ\rho and δ=δ′∘ψ\delta=\delta^{\prime}\circ\psi. Letting f:C→ℭf:C\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} be an étale cover over which ρ:S→ℭ\rho:S\rightarrow\mathfrak{C} becomes trivial, say with isomorphism θ:S×ℭC→∼C×𝔸1\theta:S\times_{\mathfrak{C}}C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}C\times\mathbb{A}^{1}, and choosing a section σ:C→C×𝔸1\sigma:C\rightarrow C\times\mathbb{A}^{1} of prC:C×𝔸1→C\mathrm{pr}_{C}:C\times\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow C, the composition ψ∘f=ψ∘f∘prC∘σ\psi\circ f=\psi\circ f\circ\mathrm{pr}_{C}\circ\sigma is equal to ψ∘ρ∘pr1∘θ−1∘σ\psi\circ\rho\circ\mathrm{pr}_{1}\circ\theta^{-1}\circ\sigma and hence to ρ′∘pr1∘θ−1∘σ\rho^{\prime}\circ\mathrm{pr}_{1}\circ\theta^{-1}\circ\sigma by construction of ψ\psi.

This implies that ψ∘f:C→ℭ′\psi\circ f:C\rightarrow\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} is a morphism whence that ψ:ℭ→ℭ′\psi:\mathfrak{C}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} is a morphism since being a morphism is a local property with respect to the étale topology. The same argument on an étale cover f′:C′→ℭ′f^{\prime}:C^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} over which ρ′:S′→ℭ′\rho^{\prime}:S^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} becomes trivial implies that the set-theoretic inverse ψ−1\psi^{-1} of ψ\psi is also a morphism, and so ψ:ℭ→ℭ′\psi:\mathfrak{C}\rightarrow\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} is an isomorphism of spaces over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}.

3.5.

In what follows, given an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibered surface π:S→ℙ1\pi:S\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}, we use the notation S/𝔸1S/\mathbb{A}^{1} to refer to an algebraic space δ:ℭ→ℙ1\delta:\mathfrak{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with the property that π\pi factors through an étale locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle ρ:S→ℭ\rho:S\rightarrow\mathfrak{C}. The previous observation implies that its existence is a local problem with respect to the Zariski topology on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. More precisely, we may cover ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} by finitely many affine open subsets UiU_{i}, i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r over which the restriction of π:S→ℙ1\pi:S\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration with a most a degenerate fiber, say π−1​(pi)\pi^{-1}(p_{i}) for some pi∈Uip_{i}\in U_{i}. Since the restriction of π\pi over Ui,∗=Ui∖{pi}U_{i,*}=U_{i}\setminus\left\{p_{i}\right\} is then a Zariski locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle, we see that if δi:ℭi=π−1​(Ui)/𝔸1→Ui\delta_{i}:\mathfrak{C}_{i}=\pi^{-1}(U_{i})/\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow U_{i} exists then the restriction of δi\delta_{i} over Ui∖{pi}U_{i}\setminus\left\{p_{i}\right\} is an isomorphism of schemes over UiU_{i}. This implies that the isomorphisms δj−1∘δi∣δ−1​(Ui,∗∩Uj,∗):δi−1​(Ui,∗∩Uj,∗)→δj−1​(Ui,∗∩Uj,∗)\delta_{j}^{-1}\circ\delta_{i}\mid_{\delta^{-1}(U_{i,*}\cap U_{j,*})}:\delta_{i}^{-1}(U_{i,*}\cap U_{j,*})\rightarrow\delta_{j}^{-1}(U_{i,*}\cap U_{j,*}), i,j=1,…,ri,j=1,\ldots,r, satisfy the usual cocyle condition on triple intersections whence that the algebraic space δ:ℭ=S/𝔸1→ℙ1\delta:\mathfrak{C}=S/\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with the desired property is obtained by gluing the local ones δi:ℭi→Ui\delta_{i}:\mathfrak{C}_{i}\rightarrow U_{i}, i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r along their respective open sub-schemes δi−1​(Ui,∗∩Uj,∗)⊂ℭi\delta_{i}^{-1}(U_{i,*}\cap U_{j,*})\subset\mathfrak{C}_{i}, i,j=1,…,ri,j=1,\ldots,r via these isomorphisms.

3.6.
